tip: Dovremmo is the conditional of dovere and turns duty into advice: dovremmo partire = we should leave, softer than dobbiamo (we must).
Di più means 'more' and comes after the verb: riposare di più = rest more, never 'più riposare'.
Saresti is the conditional of essere (would be) and softens questions: saresti disponibile? = would you be available?
Condizionale passato means would or could have: it pairs the conditional of avere or essere with a participle, so avresti potuto = you could have.
Avremmo dovuto expresses regret about the past, our 'should have': the conditional of avere plus dovuto, then the infinitive prenotare.
Potremmo, the conditional of potere, makes a request polite: potremmo avere il conto? = could we have the bill? gentler than possiamo.
Frutta is a feminine collective noun and stays singular even for many pieces: più frutta = more fruit, not 'frutte'.
Vorremmo is the polite 'we would like', softer than vogliamo (we want): vorremmo ordinare = we would like to order.
Italian pairs fare (to do) with exercise: fare esercizio = to exercise, literally 'do exercise'.
Plural family words keep the article with a possessive: i miei figli = my children. The article drops only with a singular relative, like mio figlio.
Andare has an irregular conditional stem andr-: andresti = you would go, not 'anderesti'.
Secondo me means 'in my opinion', literally 'according to me', the everyday way to open an opinion.
An object pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive: dire plus lo becomes dirlo (say it), and dire drops its final -e.
The preposition a merges with the article la into alla: alla festa = to the party.
Problema is masculine despite the -a ending, a Greek-origin word: il problema, i problemi. Same for tema and sistema.
Subject pronouns are usually dropped, so adding noi adds emphasis: noi siamo ottimisti stresses 'we'. Plain siamo ottimisti is enough.
The present tense works as a casual request: mi presti la penna? = will you lend me the pen? No future tense needed.
Ci sono means 'there are' (plural); c'è means 'there is' (singular). Many tourists takes ci sono: ci sono molti turisti.
Adjectives ending in -e like triste do not change for gender: a man or a woman is equally triste.
Rimanere takes essere, so its participle agrees with the subject: pochi posti sono rimasti = few seats are left.
Forse (maybe) keeps the normal indicative or conditional, no subjunctive: forse dovremmo partire = maybe we should leave.
Essere forms its own past with itself as the helper: siamo stati = we have been, and stati agrees with the plural subject.
With avere as helper the participle stays fixed: hanno avuto (never 'avuti'), no matter the subject.
Spendere has the irregular participle speso: hanno speso = they spent, not 'spenduto'.
The ending -issimo means very or extremely: gentilissimi = extremely kind, stronger than molto gentili.
The imperfetto describes repeated past habits: uscivi ogni sera = you used to go out every evening.
After essere the participle agrees with the subject: a woman è scesa (feminine), a man è sceso. Scendere gives sceso.
Bere keeps its older stem bev- in the imperfetto: bevevo = I used to drink.
Weather uses fare: faceva caldo = it was hot, literally 'it made heat'. Also fare freddo for cold.
Ci (there) attaches to the end of a let's-form: andiamo plus ci becomes andiamoci = let's go there.
